The belief: a widget is the thing you see.

It's a natural assumption. In most UI toolkits, "widget" means exactly that: a long-lived control with properties you mutate. Flutter code reads like it constructs those objects, the DevTools inspector shows a widget tree that mirrors the screen, and the name
sounds like the widget itself holds state. The half-truth is the structure: the widget tree does describe what's on screen. It just doesn't stay there.
Flutter keeps three trees side by side, and each one has a different job.
The API docs define a widget as something that "describes the configuration for an Element", and its fields must all be final: widgets follow
. The Flutter docs call them temporary objects, used to build a presentation of the app in its current state. Every call to

returns brand-new widget objects, and the previous ones are dropped. That's affordable because a widget is a small bundle of constructor arguments, not a view. The same widget object can even be placed in the tree several times.
Elements: the instance at a place in the tree

A render object widget copies its new configuration onto the existing render object, so a changed color or padding is an update in place, not a new object.
If the type or key differs, the old element and everything below it is removed, and a new one is created from the new widget.
If the new widget is the very same instance as last time, as
widgets often are, the walk stops there.

items.title: Stop worrying about creating widgets in build()

content.text: New widget objects on every build are the design, not a leak. Worry about expensive work inside
constructors where you can so Flutter can skip unchanged subtrees.
